questions.prompt: A data analyst plans six report tasks. Sort them by whether real rows from the samples database would leave the machine.
questions.explain: Text you type, schemas and invented rows keep real data home. Pasting, uploading or letting an agent read data sends it, even when the tool is read-only.

items.text: Ask for an outline and section headings for a quarterly report
items.misconception: A question with no data in it sends only the words you typed.

items.text: Paste the schema and ask for a query that you run yourself
items.misconception: Table and column names travel and the rows stay on your machine, because you run the query.

items.text: Ask how to explain a fall in sample numbers to a board
items.misconception: A general question needs no data, so nothing from the database is sent.

items.text: Upload the whole sample table so the model can count by project
items.misconception: An upload is sent to the provider like pasted text, however helpful the count is.

items.text: Paste ten rows with participant codes to get counts by month
items.misconception: Pasted rows are sent, and codes that replace names are still personal data.

items.text: Let a read-only agent open the data folder and summarise it
items.misconception: Read-only limits what the agent changes. It still sends what it reads.

questions.prompt: A data analyst runs an agent in plan mode on a copy of the database. What does the read-only part protect them from?
questions.explain: Plan mode limits what the agent does. Reading still happens, so the contents it reads are sent to the provider.

options.text: Edits to your files, while what the agent reads is still sent
Anything leaving the machine, because a read-only agent cannot write anything
options.misconception: Read-only restricts actions. Reading is the step that sends data.

options.text: Network use, because plan mode blocks calls to outside services
options.misconception: Plan mode limits actions such as editing. It has no say over where the content it reads is sent.

questions.prompt: The model's query ran without an error and reports 22 samples for Heron. Your own count query says 11. What is the sensible next move?
questions.explain: Neither number is trusted until you know why they differ. Here a join repeats each sample once per open milestone.

options.text: Find out why the two differ before using either number
Ask the model whether it is sure, then use its answer
options.misconception: A fluent yes from the same model checks nothing.

options.text: Average the two numbers, since both could be partly right
options.misconception: An average of a wrong count and a right one is still wrong. Find which is right.

options.text: Use the model's number, since it ran without an error
options.misconception: Running without an error says nothing about correctness.

questions.prompt: Match each step to what leaves your machine.
questions.explain: The step sets what the tool can do, and what you type, paste, upload or let it read sets what leaves.

pairs.misconception: With no data in the prompt, only your own wording is sent.

pairs.left: Chat with schema or headings and invented rows
pairs.right: Names and headings, and the invented rows
pairs.misconception: The shape of the data goes, and the real rows stay with you.

pairs.left: Local model on the real data
pairs.right: Nothing, unless a web or tool call sends something
pairs.misconception: A local model keeps prompts home, and tools it calls may still reach out.
A copy protects the original from edits, and the copy's contents are still sent when read.

questions.prompt: The organisation pays for an organisation account. A colleague wants to use a personal Pro account for the same report data. What matters most?
questions.explain: The two kinds of account have different documented terms, such as the training setting and retention. Use the account your organisation approved for that data.

options.text: The terms may differ by account type, so use the approved one
The terms are the same, because both accounts talk to the same model
options.misconception: Terms belong to the plan and the account type, and the model name does not decide them.

options.text: A personal account is safer, because no administrator is involved in it
options.misconception: Fewer people involved does not make an account approved for that data.

questions.prompt: Which statement about incognito chats is correct?
questions.explain: Incognito chats are not used for training and are still kept for 30 days by default, so they are not a place for data that must never leave.

options.text: Not used for training, and still kept for 30 days by default
They leave nothing on the provider's side once the chat has ended
options.misconception: The page gives a 30-day default retention.

options.text: They are deleted from the provider as soon as the window closes
options.misconception: Deletion takes up to 30 days, and flagged chats may be kept longer.

questions.prompt: A manager wants a formula that counts open milestones per project in a spreadsheet. Which prompt keeps the real rows at home?
questions.explain: Column headings and a few invented rows are enough for a model to write a formula. You apply it to the real sheet yourself.

options.text: Paste headings and three invented rows; apply the formula yourself
Upload the whole workbook so the formula fits the real data exactly
options.misconception: An upload is sent to the provider like pasted text, so the real rows leave.

options.text: Paste the real rows for one project to test it, and keep the rest back
options.misconception: Those rows still leave, and a status list can name people.
